analysis.one_liner: Exempts banks and credit unions with under $50 billion in assets from all Consumer Financial Protection Bureau rules.
analysis.headline: The bill cleared the House Financial Services Committee on a 30-25 vote in 2018 but never received a vote by the full House before Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would free nearly all banks and credit unions — every insured depository institution or credit union with less than $50 billion in assets, which covers almost the entire banking industry — from every rule the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau issues. The CFPB writes and enforces rules meant to protect consumers in areas like mortgages, credit cards, and debt collection. Under the bill, the bureau could only reapply a rule to exempted institutions if it proved a pattern of consumer harm and got written agreement from every federal banking agency.
analysis.who_benefits: Banks and credit unions with under $50 billion in assets gain relief from complying with CFPB consumer-protection rules, which the industry describes as a significant compliance cost. Only the handful of institutions above $50 billion would remain subject to the bureau's rules [S2][S3][S4].
analysis.who_benefits_short: Small and mid-sized banks and credit unions

how_it_helps.text: Exempts any insured depository institution or credit union with less than $50 billion in consolidated assets from all rules and regulations issued by the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau [S3][S4].

The exemption applies prospectively to rules issued or modified after enactment, and the bureau could not modify prior rules for exempted institutions unless the modification expanded an exemption or reduced compliance costs [S4].

analysis.who_pays: Bank customers would lose the CFPB's consumer protections at nearly every bank and credit union they use, since the exemption covers all but the largest institutions. Reapplying a rule to an exempted class of institutions would require the bureau to prove a pattern of consumer harm and win written agreement from every federal banking agency, a high hurdle [S3][S4].
analysis.who_pays_short: Customers of nearly all banks and credit unions

drawbacks.text: Because nearly all banks and credit unions fall under the $50 billion threshold, the bill would strip consumer-protection rules from almost the entire banking industry, leaving only the largest institutions covered [S2][S3].

The revocation process is demanding: the bureau must make a detailed written finding that a class of institutions engaged in a pattern or practice of activity detrimental to consumers, and each federal banking agency must agree in writing [S4].

The exemption begins only with rules issued or modified after enactment, but it blocks the bureau from tightening prior rules for exempted institutions, so existing protections could not be strengthened for them [S4].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: Compliance-cost relief for community banks is a real and widely cited benefit, but the design is sweeping: rather than tailoring rules to institutions' size or risk, it removes the CFPB's consumer-protection jurisdiction from virtually the whole industry, and the only mechanism for restoring a rule requires proof of a 'pattern or practice' of harm plus the agreement of every federal banking regulator. The consumer-protection cost falls on ordinary bank customers, who would be covered by CFPB rules only at a handful of very large banks.

outcome.mechanism: The Financial Services Committee approved the bill on a 30-25 vote and it was placed on the House calendar in August 2018, but House leaders never brought it to the floor for a vote before that Congress ended in January 2019.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced by Rep. Roger Williams on February 28, 2017 and referred to the House Committee on Financial Services [S1][S6].
The subcommittee held hearings in January 2018, and the full committee ordered the bill reported in amended form by a 30-25 vote on January 18, 2018 [S6].
The committee reported the amended bill on August 3, 2018, with a report number of H. Rept. 115-885, and it was placed on the Union Calendar [S3][S4][S6].
No further action was taken; the bill sat on the calendar until the 115th Congress ended on January 3, 2019, without a House floor vote [S1][S6].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Bank customers are better off than they would have been under the bill, because the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau's rules continue to apply to nearly all banks and credit unions. Banks seeking relief from the bureau's rules did not get it.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Bank customers, not the banking industry

for.name: Rep. Roger Williams
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and assembled 30 Republican cosponsors for it.

for.name: House Financial Services Committee
for.what_they_did: Held hearings and a markup, then reported the bill in amended form on a 30-25 vote.

against.name: House Republican leadership
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled the bill for a vote by the full House after it was placed on the calendar in August 2018, leaving it to die at the end of the Congress.

sides.party_line_note: All 30 cosponsors were Republicans, and the committee vote of 30-25 split along party lines on a committee the Republicans chaired [S5][S6].

industries.industry: Community banks and credit unions (under $50 billion in assets)
industries.note: The bill would free nearly every bank and credit union from all CFPB consumer-protection rules, eliminating compliance costs. The cost falls on their customers, who would lose federal consumer protections at almost every institution they use.

The largest institutions would remain the only ones subject to CFPB rules, leaving them with compliance costs their smaller competitors would not face. They would remain the only institutions whose customers keep the bureau's protections.
